subtopic: MR. HERRIDGE    CRITICISM OF PUBLIC SERVANTS BY MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
MR. HERRIDGE    CRITICISM OF PUBLIC SERVANTS BY MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. My point of privilege is based on the fact that in my opinion certain statements made by one H. L. Keenleyside in the press are a challenge to the ancient rights and privileges of members of parliament. When Mr. Keenleyside was giving evidence before the external affairs committee on the Columbia river treaty, he stated in his closing remarks as follows:
I believe I am justified in objecting most strongly to the sneering attacks that have been made on these senior officials and highly competent technical advisers, attacks which are, in my opinion, as unjust in substance and as deplorable in taste as they are constitutionally improper.
My question of privilege is based on a letter appearing in the Ottawa Citizen on Tuesday, April 21, 1964, written by one H. L. Keenleyside and entitled "Attacks on public servants in the house are deplored", in which he restated at much greater length the substance of the statement made before the external affairs committee.
It is obvious that H. L. Keenleyside's remarks are directed at me. That is of little consequence to me, as I am quite capable of defending myself against such a charge. However, in my opinion, Mr. Speaker, and in the opinion of a good number of other members, this is a challenge to the rights of all members of this house, and I feel duty bound to bring it to the attention of the house.
Now, I understand that in rising on a question of privilege it is proper for a member to state his point of privilege. I have done that. Then the member must produce prima facie evidence to support his point of privilege, and I shall do that. Then it is customary for the member to move a motion. Therefore I now proceed to produce my evidence in support of my point of privilege, which is based on Dr. H. L. Keenleyside's letter in the Ottawa Citizen of April 21, 1964.
The questions at issue, Mr. Speaker, are first, whether a member of the Commons may freely and constitutionally comment, in the house or in a committee thereof, on the conduct of any person in the public service
in so far as that conduct relates to such person's official duties. Second, whether any person may criticize a member for so commenting and not be in contempt of the house. The answers to these questions are fully contained in certain resolutions unanimously confirmed by the United Kingdom House of Commons on February 26, 1701. The relevant extract from the orders of the House of Commons, second edition, 1756, is as follows:
Colonel Granvil reported from the committee of the whole house, to consider further of the rights, liberties, and privileges of the House of Commons, that they had come to several resolutions, which they had directed him to report, when the house will please to receive the same.
The report ordered to be read immediately, and he reported, viz.
First, resolved, that it is the opinion of this committee, that to assert that the House of Commons is not the only representative of the Commons of England, tends to the subversion of the rights and privileges of the House of Commons, and the fundamental constitution of the government of this kingdom.
Second, resolved, that it is the opinion of this committee, that to assert, that the House of Commons have no power of commitment, but of their own members, tehds to the subversion of the constitution of the House of Commons.
Third, resolved, that it is the opinion of this committee, that to print or publish any books or libels reflecting on the proceedings of the House of Commons, or any member thereof, for, or relating to, his service therein, is a high violation of the rights and privileges of the House of Commons.
Fourth, resolved, that it is, and ever hath been the undoubted right of the subjects of England, to petition the King for the calling and sitting of parliaments, and redressing of grievances. That to traduce such petitioning, as a violation of duty, and to represent it to his Majesty, as seditious and tumultuous, is to betray the liberty of the subject, and contributes to the designs of subverting the ancient legal constitution of this kingdom, and introducing arbitrary power.
Fifth, resolved, that it is the opinion of this committee, that it is the undoubted right of every subject of England, under any accusation, either by impeachment or otherwise, to be brought to a speedy trial, in order to be acquitted or condemned.
The said resolutions being severally read a second time, were, upon the question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the house.
Under the protection of the privileges, Mr. Speaker, a member can properly criticize a member of the public service in the performance of his public duties and is protected when he does so. Further, upon a criticism made, the House of Commons had jurisdiction to adjudicate upon the charge so made and to administer punishment upon conviction.
A complaint is made under the fourth resolution as a grievance. This right is that of every subject. The grievance can originate

Question of Privilege
with the member himself in his capacity as a subject or, under the first resolution, as a representative of the commoners or subjects of England. Under the fifth resolution, the subject so accused is entitled to a speedy trial -by the house if it assumes jurisdiction-to be acquitted or condemned. And, if condemned, then under the second resolution he can be committed by the house to prison although he is not a member of the house.
I am not going to read at length from the very interesting precedent here, but there is another interesting precedent to be found in Gray's debates of the House of Commons for 1667 to 1694, volume VI, at page 153. Now, Mr. Speaker, this precedent I have just referred to illustrates the constitutional position. Every citizen, member of the house or not, by petition under our standing order 70, or orally by or through a member in a proper proceeding, as on supply, can charge a crown employee before the house with misconduct or negligence in office. The house may investigate the charge, adjudicate the charge, and acquit or condemn the employee.
In 1964 the constitutional position is the same in the Canadian House of Commons as it was in England in 1701. Certain of these privileges have been delegated but can be repossessed at any time by parliamentary action.
The present day procedural position is that by section 18 of the British North America Act and section 4 of the Senate and House of Commons Act, this House of Commons and the members thereof have the privileges of the United Kingdom House of Commons as of 1867. These privileges can be cut down, varied, but not increased by Canadian statute. Two Canadian statutes vary the privileges of the house as to investigation, adjudication and consequent acquittal or condemnation. The criminal aspects of abuse of office are not here dealt with. The two statutes are an act respecting public and department inquiries, 1952 revised statutes, chapter 154, and the Civil Service Act, 1960-61 acts, chapter 57.

1.	On the Canadian National Railway, what percentage increase in passenger service resulted from the new fare program currently known as the red, white and blue plan?
2.	What percentage increase has resulted in each area?
3.	What extra costs are necessary to handle the increased passenger traffic?

The management of Canadian National Railways advises that it is not possible to answer the question categorically in the form asked. The following information is supplied:
The first test of the red, white and blue fare plan was carried out on lines east of Montreal to the maritimes, commencing May 1, 1962. The reaction to the fare changes was very encouraging and significant increases in traffic and revenues were achieved in 1962 compared with the previous year, despite less passenger train miles being operated in 1962 than in 1961.
On May 1, 1963, some slight revisions were made to the original plan as a result of experience and the fares were extended indefinitely in the maritime territory; at the same time they were offered in Newfoundland. On June 23, 1963, the new rates were introduced between Toronto and North Bay and in

Questions
conjunction with the Ontario Northland Railway to points in northern Ontario. The new fare system was brought into effect on the transcontinental route, on local services in western Canada and in southwestern Ontario, effective October 27, 1963.
As shown in the 1963 annual report, the downward trends in traffic and revenues of recent years were halted in 1962 and reversed in 1963. During 1963 the total number of revenue passengers carried increased 9.3 per cent from 12.4 million to 13.6 million. The number of passengers carried one mile, or revenue passenger miles, increased by 13.9 per cent from 1.0 billion to 1.2 billion. Total rail revenue derived from the transportation of passengers (fare, accommodation, meals and miscellaneous) increased by almost $1,000,000 from 1961 to 1963, a two year period when total passenger train miles operated were decreased by slightly in excess of 13 per cent.
By and large, increases in traffic and in revenues have occurred whenever and wherever the new fares have been introduced. They have also increased traffic in adjoining
or non-red, white and blue territories by encouraging through or connecting traffic.
The level of charges under red, white and blue is such as to encourage the largest increase in passenger travel, relative to the cost of providing the service. The relation of revenues to expenses of operation is expected to be more favourable under this fare plan than under others.
Detailed results obtaining in any given territory and other similar data have not been released publicly, for competitive reasons.

subtopic: RESTRICTIONS ON DUMPING OF WASTE INTO GREAT LAKES
speechtext:
The oil pollution prevention regulations provide that no person shall discharge or allow to escape from a ship into the inland, minor or other waters of Canada any oil or oily mixture that foul the surface of the water, and oil includes crude oil, fuel oil, heavy diesel oil, lubricating oil, vegetable oil, fish or other fatty oils.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, the ubiquitous Minister of Transport has misconstrued the remarks I made. I said there were rumours that this was happening, but I am not suggesting it was illegal or in contravention of the act.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Neither did I.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
All right. I am making a point, and if the representation commissioner has been at work as authorized and directed by parliament, then that is fine. I am not questioning that. What I am saying is that there are rumours or reports that the maps have already been prepared, and what I am questioning is, by whom? Who are the people doing this and what are their qualifications for the preparation of these maps?
If this be the case, under these circumstances whether it be the commission set up under the proposed amendment or even under the act, are we not authorizing some sort of a blank cheque and suggesting that these provincial commissions shall be rubber stamps? If the thing is going to be all cut and dried for them beforehand, then why set them up? At least, why set them up with this sort of aura of independence, or independence from any political implication. Why suggest there is anything wrong with political connections in regard to bodies set up by parliament? After all, everything we do is political. The administration of this country is political. This is the science of government and the active carrying out of it. So, why is there all this sanctimonious clap-trap we sometimes read in comments about this
[Mr. Lambert.!
house, that the people here are somehow second rate persons because they are politicians?
Who on earth can set himself up at that level to downgrade persons who take an interest in public affairs in this house, in provincial legislatures and in municipal government? If the people making these comments had the courage of their convictions, why don't they get out into this business of politics and find out for themselves? I apologize, Mr. Chairman, for these perhaps intemperate remarks, but I think we have had enough of such comments.
It is true enough that this body must be subject to criticism, but let us not have it from high and mighty towers. The people who have served this country in public life in the past, who are serving it in the present and who will serve it in the future, without assuming any mantle or halo of self-justification, have been, are, and will be discharging their duties as citizens.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Unless anyone can point the finger and come up with proof of venality with regard to participation in public life, then I would say to him, in the very crude phrase, "either put up or shut up."
Now, having said that, I have asked the question, who is preparing these maps, what are their qualifications, and is there any means of examining them before we give this blank cheque? After all, the purport of the amendment is to remove this entirely from parliament and, if we look at the bill, there is but a tenuous connection with parliament thereafter.	-
There is no obligation for public hearings. Clause 17 is only permissive and, if I may be permitted to make a little further reference to clause 17, by the provisions of subsections 2 and 4 of that clause only five days are allowed for a person or body to make up their mind to study the report of the commission and to file their objections, provided the commission has deemed that it shall hold public hearings.
I shall have a lot more to say about clause 17, which provides that notice be published in the Canada Gazette 15 days prior to the hearings, with the further requirement that the secretary of the commission shall have ten days' notice before the hearings. The gist and purport of this is that there will only be five days for anyone in any province to make representations against the decisions of a commission. In effect this is almost tantamount to a denial of review.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
May I ask the hon. gentleman a question. He started out by referring

maintopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Well, I am glad to see that the minister is giving us a tip, but I do not know whether it is a Pandora's box from which he has tried to lift just a corner of the lid, or whether it has been like holding out a paper bag to children and saying maybe there is some candy in it. I have not heard the rumour, but we have now got it from the horse's mouth.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION

maintopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: I am glad the hon. member has made a speech because it gives me 30 minutes from now in which to speak, but I fail to see how this is a point of order.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, on the point of order, I should like to support the right of the hon. member for Edmonton West to speak for 30 minutes from now, provided he is on clause 6.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: I am coming to clause 6. I have indicated the difficulties involved in the hearings and I beg the indulgence of the house in order to do so. If these maps and so forth are ready, let us know what they are at this time. What are the objections if the work is already done? It would give an indication to hon. members how the composition of the house may be affected, and members are no less entitled than anyone else to this information since it affects their rights as citizens and as well as members of the house who may be adversely affected within their constituencies. Is there not a danger under the present set-up of the commission actually being almost in the nature of a rubber stamp?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: That is right.

I raise this as a danger signal. maintopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether I could raise a point of order? I would not raise it perhaps against any other member of the house, but the hon. member for Edmonton West is a former Speaker of the house and as a former Speaker perhaps he should set the rest of us an example in obeying the rules. At the last session of parliament we did establish a position. It was established by parliament and certain duties were laid down in clause 8 of the statute. I made a mistake in the clause before because I had picked up the act quickly. But it does seem to me, Mr. Chairman, that when parliament has laid down the conditions under which the job is to be done it is surely a reflection upon parliament itself to suggest that the person doing the job is doing something that is in some way improper. I do not believe the hon. member for Edmonton West recollects what clause 8 of the act contains, and I wonder whether I might permitted to read it so that we will be talking-

maintopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, what is the point of order? Otherwise the minister is out of order in standing up.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: My point of order, very briefly, is that we are dealing with clause 6 of the present bill, and instead of dealing with clause 6 of the bill the hon. gentleman is debating a matter which relates to an act of parliament already passed. I suggest that in doing so he is going beyond the scope of clause 6 and is giving the impression that something which parliament ordered an officer of parliament to do he should not be doing.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I should like to speak to the point of order. It seems to me that what the minister is really saying is that we have got to confine our arguments solely to clause 6. I do not see how we can confine our arguments strictly to the wording of clause 6 because clause 6 cannot be read separately and apart without considering many other sections of the bill and the other act involved. I would say that the member who has the floor has been absolutely in order and the debate should continue.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, with regard to the argument raised on the point of order, if the Minister of Transport would tame his impatience he would see that within the framework of the amendment there is a reference to the representation commissioner and I am reviewing the position of the representation commissioner under the act appointing him. Nowhere can the minister detect any objection on my part to the representation commissioner and the work he

Electoral Boundaries Commission has done so far. What I am concerned about is the amendment.
I am advancing my argument somewhat, but if you look at paragraph (b) of subclause (b) of the amendment you will see that the chief justice of the province is directed to appoint certain persons in the alternative after consultation with the representation commissioner. So far as the designated persons are concerned the chief justice has authority to act without reference to the representation commissioner, but when he has to go beyond that category he must refer to the representation commissioner. I suggest to hon. members that that provision is repugnant. I do not see why there should be this provision for reference to the representation commissioner.
It seems to me we are blithely building up a framework in which there is not that check and counterbalance that there should be. Frankly, we are setting up almost an autocratic organization under the representation commissioner. First of all, we have the act setting up the office and directing the representation commissioner to do certain work. He goes ahead with his staff to do that work. We do not know the qualifications of the members of his staff, whether they are geographers or political scientists or what. Who are they? We would like to know that.
This framework is set up and then the chief justice of the province is to appoint the commissioners for the province from among certain individuals. But in default of a province agreeing that certain employees of the province shall act on the federal commission the chief justice is directed to appoint alternates after consultation with the representation commissioner. I do not believe that such a requirement is satisfactory. If the chief justice is a satisfactory person to make these appointments otherwise, then why should there be provision for the consent or approval of the representation commissioner with regard to nominations to the commission in certain circumstances?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: That allows the minister to get his hand in.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: After all, this means that the representation commissioner has the right to say who shall sit on a commission with him, because actually he is a member of every provincial commission. I do not believe that framework is right in this regard. After all, the chief justice is not authorized to name himself on the commission. The provision indicates that he shall name someone from among the judges under his jurisdiction. I find it rather difficult to understand otherwise under this type of legislation whereby the chief justice does say: I name you.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Yes, I do too.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
This, under the ordinary interpretation of language would be a direction to pick from amongst the members of his court or, under the subamendment, from any of the superior courts. If the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre would distinctly understand the composition of our superior courts, he would know that there is a trial division and an appellate division. The trial division has a chief justice and as a result the chief justice of the province has a limited jurisdiction over all judges. Is he able to say, also, that he will name himself? I do not think so. He is therefore going to name another justice who is a member of a court under his jurisdiction.
So, we have this disqualification of the chief justice and the provision saying that he cannot name outright all the commissioners. I believe this would be right because otherwise we would be telling the chief justice: "You name the people that you want", and if you do that you set up in fact, if not in theory, a one-man representation commission. This could be a possibility; but the act, as I say, does provide against that.
Now, on the other hand, if a province denies the right of its public officials to membership on the representation commission, the chief justice must then come back to the representation commissioner, who is a member of the commission under this act, for the approval of the appointment of another member to the commission. I do not believe that is logical.
I come to my third point. In view of the work that has been done by the representation commissioner and his staff, under the act authorizing them to do it, and the plans that are prepared for submission to the representation commissioner, I would put it to hon. members that the tolerance formula may become quite academic. I do say that I would much rather see some more independent persons named by the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition, who may work as a check and countercheck. Somebody has said we are trying to divorce this from politics. I do not believe there is a man in public life who is entirely divorced from politics, even with all the intentions to be so. I would say that, in my opinion, there is an important factor in the check and countercheck, and that greater justice will not only be done but will appear to be done under the formula provided for in the bill.
The government did not come to this conclusion hastily. I am sure that the then secretary of state was not flying trial balloons to sound out the opinion of the house and of

the public when he advanced such suggestions. He must have received a pretty good echo of the provision which he recommended to his cabinet colleagues. Knowing the Minister of Transport, I know the care he would take in advising his colleagues on this particular key provision of the bill. His cabinet colleagues have accepted this, and they must be fixed with the responsibility therefor. It was not something that had been suggested very lightly. It was not a suggestion that was made within the famous 60 days of decision. This has been very carefully considered legislation, with the exception of what I will have to say later on about clause 17. There is always the possibility that it only takes one word to change and greatly improve legislation.
I say this is not the way, by making this complete change, to get away from partisan political action. I would say that the danger of having a more partisan commission might arise under the formula devised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I say that when we get into the academic staffs of the universities, there are some gentlemen there who will fight to the death for the right to assert their partisan political views. They do so on every occasion. We see them day after day on television and radio. Some of them also have taken charge of the political activities in certain of these provinces. I know this is so in the province of Saskatchewan, and their federal campaign was pretty well in the hands of academics.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Was that the reason the results were so good?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: The fact that they are at the academic level does not detract from their political activity, and I would not want it to. Let us not say we are making these political academics into political eunuchs by any means.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: I wonder if the hon. gentleman would allow me to ask him a question? Does he think the people who might be recommended by my right hon. friend the Prime Minister or by his right hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition would be political eunuchs?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
No, because I do not think there are such people. I said it was not the extension of this aura of political purity that is improper. This amendment that we are considering is not going to create political eunuchs; I do not think you can find one. There is no such political purity. There is no advantage gained by the acceptance of such an amendment. There is a far better chance of justice under the original provision. These are the further criticisms that I have.
Electoral Boundaries Commission This is what concerned me. There would be this particular body erected under a framework which could result in a rubber stamp set-up because of the illogical structure. After all, the commission could dispense with a hearing. I think this is one danger and I am hoping the Minister of Transport may bring forward a viable amendment to clause 17 which would perhaps remove this disability. In any event, I think the original proposal in the bill is a far better formula than that proposed in the amendment.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: I must say that with many of the things said by the hon. member for Edmonton West I cannot disagree very much. As to the idea that we must try to get political eunuchs, whatever they are-I suppose, in a sense, since the hon. gentleman imported that term, judges are, because they are not allowed to vote. But I think there is a great deal of difference between politics, as the hon. gentleman used the word in the beginning of his statement, and politics in a more partisan sense. After all, the reason we want to have a commission to carry out redistribution is not to get it away from politics, in the broad sense of that word, but to get it away from party politics. If we think this job could be better done by politicians, we should scrap this legislation entirely and do it in the old-fashioned way, the way that Sir John Macdonald, that great purist, used in the past.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: And Mackenzie King.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: But I do not think anybody in the committee has seriously suggested we should do that. We feel we have made a lot of progress in this matter. It seems to me there is a very narrow point of difference in the committee at this time. I, myself, am in a difficult position because, since I indicated that I have a slight preference-and it is not very great, as I said on Friday-for the amendment, I am expected to try to find some fault with my own drafting. This puts me in a very awkward and embarrassing position, particularly when the hon. gentleman is so complimentary to me as he was this afternoon when he said that after great thought and after an exercise of great wisdom I had produced something upon which no one could improve-that clause 6, as it now stands was, indeed, all but divinely inspired. Yet it was just the best thing, up to that time, that I had been able to recommend, and that is why I recommended it.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: It still is.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Hon. gentlemen opposite say: "It still is" and I thank them for the compliment. But I was not quite so proud of my handiwork at the time when I produced

Electoral Boundaries Commission the bill originally, and with regard to this very clause, when exception was taken on second reading I said, as I have said at every stage, that if anyone could suggest an improvement, and if I thought it was an improvement, I would vote for it. That goes for every clause in this bill. Indeed, there are at least three other clauses including clause 17, to which I myself wish to propose amendments; I hope other hon. members may also have suggestions for improvements and I can assure them that in such a case they will not face any stonewalling on this side of the house. But I do not think this particular clause is perfect, by any means. It was just the best one I could figure out. I notice that the hon. member for Edmonton West said that while clause 6 was perfect some of the other clauses were open to question. Apparently, if he agrees with a clause it is wise, and if he does not agree with it it is not so wise.
In order to remove any doubt, in the light of what has been said in this discussion, I think I should be permitted to read section 8 of the act respecting the office of representation commissioner which lays down clearly what the representation commissioner was instructed by this parliament to do. I think we ought to have this clearly in our minds. It reads as follows:
As soon as possible after the completion of any decennial census-
That, of course, really applies to the future.
-or in the case of the census taken in 1961 as soon as possible after the coming into force of this act, the commissioner shall prepare maps showing the distribution of population in each province and setting out alternative proposals-
And I stress that word "alternative"-
-respecting the boundaries of electoral districts in each province and shall thereupon supply such maps to the appropriate electoral boundaries commission.
I understand that as far as it is possible for the representation commissioner to carry out that instruction-and it is not entirely possible, for the good reason that until parliament decides what the tolerance will be, any maps which may be drawn can only be drawn up very tentatively-

maintopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Would the hon. gentleman permit me to ask him a question? He appears to lay a good deal of stress on this matter of the tolerance. Does he not agree that though the figure in the bill may be 20 per cent the actual tolerance might be as low as 1 per cent or as high as 19 per cent, and that this tolerance provision is not as effective in protecting rural constituencies as the hon. gentleman would lead the committee to

believe. It is an academic thing and it does not mean anything when you get down to it.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: I do not think I agree with that. If I did agree with it I would wonder why the hon. gentleman and his friends have spent such a long time talking about it. It seems to me that the tolerance ought to be high enough-and in my opinion it ought to be higher at this time than may eventually be desirable when the pattern has been more or less established after one or two redistributions-for the express purpose of enabling these commissions to take the proper account of municipal boundaries, the distribution of urban and rural populations, of traditional considerations and other such factors. The hon. member for Bow River seems impatient to rise. Perhaps he would allow me to answer one question before he asks another. If we were doing all this in a mechanistic way, as the reformers did it during the French revolution, we would simply take a map and draw lines on it without any regard to whether there were human beings involved or not. But since we have chosen to approach this question in an entirely different way we must have a tolerance large enough to take account of our history and geography as well as of certain traditional factors. Quite frankly, though we had to put some figure in the bill to start with, that, like other aspects of this measure is something upon which our minds are not closed.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Perhaps I may ask a further question. We may get a tolerance of 20 per cent, or whatever is decided on. But is it not a fact that there is no safeguard written into the law to provide that the commissioners, or the people doing the work of these commissions must have regard to a 20 per cent tolerance in certain areas. It could be less than 2 per cent. So this tolerance figure becomes extremely academic. That is my question.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
That is not a question; that is an assertion, as the hon. gentleman will find out if he looks at it later. It is an assertion that the commissions are not going to pay any attention to parliament and I do not believe that if parliament were to change the figure from the figure presently in this bill to another figure, that the decision of parliament in this respect would be ignored. I am sure the change would be an indication that the majority in this parliament felt there are cases where the higher tolerance should be regarded. Otherwise, what would be the sense of putting it there?

I am quite sure that the men who are going to be appointed to these commissions, no matter which of the two methods now under discussion may be followed, are the kind of men who are not going to try to disregard the will of parliament but are going to try to carry it out. But surely the hon. member is not suggesting that this parliament should direct the commissions that they must have one constituency at the bottom of the scale of the tolerance and another at the top. Surely if we are going to have a non-partisan redistribution, we are not going to try by the back door to prevent a non-partisan redistribution. It seems to me that the implication of the hon. gentleman's assertion was that he has a secret hankering after doing the job himself, instead of leaving it to the commissions.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, that is not very fair, and I am sure the minister wants to be fair.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Yes, I want to be very fair.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: My question was this. I still believe in every safeguard for human rights or any other rights, whether under this act or any other act. That is something that is spelled out in the law. That differentiates our democratic system of the rule of law from the rule of people. What the minister is saying this afternoon is briefly this, that he has a great respect for these men, whoever they may be. No matter how high your ideals are about it, they may be subject to some elusiveness when given such wide discretion. I say that the best safeguard is to spell out a thing in the law. You can promise us or anybody else the sky, but the fact is that this protection should be given under the law and not by people, with the greatest respect to the people doing the work today.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I completely agree with that, and that is why in this bill, unlike the bill introduced by the right hon. gentleman in the last parliament, we have a definite figure for the tolerance and we do not say that the commissions can disregard the figure and take any tolerance they like. That would certainly be disregarding the law and making the commissions completely arbitrary. I am not prepared to support the abolition of the tolerance altogether. I agree with the hon. gentleman for Bow River that what the tolerance is to be should be in the law. Whatever figure the house may agree upon, it should be a definite figure beyond which the commissions cannot go; otherwise we are just handing the thing over to these commissions without any rule at all.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
maintopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, would the minister allow a question in this regard?
Electoral Boundaries Commission

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Order, please. Before the hon. member poses his question, I wonder whether I could bring to the attention of the committee that we seem to be getting away from clause 6. speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
maintopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: I agree, Mr. Chairman, and I was going to take the argument back to clause 6, in conjunction with what the minister has now said, after consideration of the tolerance. Would it not be in the interests of parliament itself, under the jurisdiction of the chief electoral officer, who is the chairman-

maintopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: The representation commissioner.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
maintopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Yes, the representation commissioner-to safeguard this particular interest in clause 6 by reverting to the initial clause in the act? maintopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
On that point, Mr. Chairman, I think perhaps I should indicate, as I indicated and as I think my colleague the Minister of Justice also indicated on Friday, that no one on this side of the house is going to try to suggest to any other hon. member what decision he should make about this matter. We do not regard this as a question of confidence at all. As I have pointed out from the beginning, it may well turn out- in fact I think it is pretty evident already- that some of us feel that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has produced a better method than the one I produced. I happen to be one of those who think so. I think, in conscience, I should support that; I think it would be an improper thing for me to support anything else. I have at no time sought to suggest to any of my friends-I refer to my political friends in the house-that they should accept my judgment; I hope they will exercise their own judgment. I even hope there may be some broadminded people on the other side of the house who will not necessarily agree with the views that have been expressed this afternoon by the hon. member for Edmonton West. But it does seem to me that we must do this one way or the other. Either we are sincere when we say that every hon. member should make up his own mind without any fear or hope of favour as to which is the best way to do this, or alternatively we have to say that this is a

Electoral Boundaries Commission government measure and the government is going to use all the discipline it knows how to get this done in a certain way.
I said on Friday, and I say again, that if the bill as originally drafted is acceptable to the house, I am not going to shed any tears over it or this clause. After all, I drafted it and I would not have brought it before the house had I thought it was bad. I do not think it is bad; I think it would work reasonably well.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Then why are you forsaking it?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Because I think the other method would be better. I know there are people in the house, and a lot of people out of the house, who do not like the idea, when we are trying to take redistribution out of politics, of having the commissions appointed, or any of the commissioners appointed, by the leaders of political parties. I do not object to that myself, but I know many, many Canadians who do; who will say that this is a second best way. I did not think we could find a better way, but I do quite honestly and genuinely feel that the amendment that has been suggested is a better way. As for the subamendment, I feel a little differently about that. Perhaps, Mr. Chairman, I could say just a word about that at this moment. In my opinion, however, even the amendment would have to be changed, but the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) and the Minister of Transport are no doubt better qualified than I am in that respect. I see, for instance, that section 6 (la) provides: "The chief electoral officer, the surveyor general or the registrar of vital statistics of the province or the holder of any similar office in the province of Quebec".
I think that we have not seen many pieces of legislation voted by this parliament using such vague and broad terms as those: "or the holder of any similar office in the province." Now, reference is made to:
1-	the chief electoral officer;
2-	the surveyor general.
Those offices are far from being similar. The chief electoral officer does not do any surveying and the surveyor general does not deal with voting on election days.
And here is a third category: "the registrar of vital statistics of the province". That is another office altogether different.
And finally, another one is added: "or the holder of any similar office in the province", while three different offices were just lined up:
1-	the chief electoral officer;
2-	the surveyor general;
3-	the registrar of vital statistics.
In my parish the parish priest is a registrar of vital statistics.
Reference is made to "the holder of any similar office". Similar to what category, Mr. Chairman? Similar to the surveyor general, to the parish priest or to the chief electoral officer?	!

[Mr. Gregoire.l
are extended remarks. The Minister of Transport has said he agrees with the original clause, but perhaps the amendment may make it a little better. I am hoping that in so doing I might persuade some of my colleagues that the original draft of this bill is the right one.
I think someone should say what I am about to say. Most members have skated around this, but let us be honest about the whole situation. What are the dangers of redistribution? Why do we find ourselves in a position where we are arguing about redistribution? Is it not simply that redistribution is a political matter?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: It is a geographical matter.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Surely no one in this house is so naive or so dishonest with himself as to say that redistribution is not a political matter. It is so darned political that we are arguing about it and probably will continue to argue about it ad infinitum. Let us not fool ourselves. If it were not a political matter, why should we be trying our best to get it outside of the bounds of partisan politics? So it is a political matter. On political matters there must be two sides

I limit it to two sides, but there are sometimes three, four or five. Basically, however, there are two sides.
If the boundaries of a constituency are drawn one way it is going to benefit one party. If they are drawn another way it is going to benefit another party. I do not say which party, and I do not say who is going to benefit. However I say this is a political matter, and let us not try to say we will be putting this into the hands of judges and others and they will not be accused of partisan politics. They cannot avoid it.
It is nearly five o'clock, but I want to say if the judges are going to be given any break at all under this legislation there must be two parties on this commission, one appointed by the Prime Minister and one appointed by the Leader of the Opposition, who will be able to put forward the opposing views in connection with redistribution. It will be necessary then for the whole commission to decide what is fair, but we cannot cripple them before they even start by not having both sides of the story laid before them. You are allowing two sides to participate in that commission, and for that reason alone we must follow the original draft of the bill.
May I call it five o'clock?
Progress reported.

speakeroldname: Mr. R. R. Souiham (Moose Mountain) moved:
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of amending the Income Tax Act, section (10), subsection (3) so that elected trustees of "larger school units" be entitled to the same exemptions of their regular indemnities for income tax purposes as those presently allowed to elected members of municipal corporations.
He said: I welcome this opportunity to direct the attention of the house to what I consider to be a defect in the income tax laws of our country. For the enlightenment of hon. members and for the sake of the record I should like to read the section to which my observations will refer. I am now holding a revised copy, office consolidation, of the Income Tax Act which at page 14, section 10(3) reads as follows-this refers to municipal officers expense allowance:
Where an elected officer of an incorporated municipality has been paid by the municipal corporation an amount as an allowance in a taxation year for expenses incident to the discharge of his duties as an elected officer of the corporation, the allowance shall not be included in computing his income for the year unless it exceeds one half of the amount that was paid to him in the year by the municipal corporation as salary or other remuneration as an elected officer of the corporation, in which event there shall be included in computing his income for the year only the amount by which the allowance exceeds one half of the amount so paid to him by way of salary or remuneration.
I think that is a clearcut enunciation of the position and I believe the problem I intend to raise will become apparent to hon. members as I continue to make a few further remarks. It is a problem which affects particularly the province of Saskatchewan inasmuch as we have there larger school units than those which exist in some of the other provinces. Back in 1905, when Saskatchewan came into confederation, we set up school districts which were very small in area; the municipal units were also relatively small. School districts in those days were four, six, or eight square miles in area. However as time went on and communications improved the areas became larger, and in 1945 the provincial government saw fit to give school districts the option of amalgamating into larger units. Thus today we have school units which comprise 30 or 40 square miles of area.
In consequence, the elected officials of these larger school units have to take possibly a whole day off from their other work in order to look after the obligations imposed on them. In order to get round these large districts 20220-158
Income Tax Act
they have to leave their businesses or vocations in charge of someone else, often at considerable expense. We believe it is time the Income Tax Act was amended in this respect so as to provide for these officials the same benefits as municipal officers now enjoy. I might say that in Saskatchewan we have some 398 municipalities the officials of which presently enjoy these benefits. Under the present legislation governing our schools we have approximately 65 of these larger school units where the duties of these officers are even greater in scope than they would normally be. In my opinion, the present provision as it affects these people is discriminatory and reflects a defect in the act.
I do not think I need take up the time of the house any further. The point I wish to make is a very simple one and I would ask members of the government to look at the act as it is drawn up at the present time, to examine the problem as far as these officials of the larger school units are concerned, and to propose an amendment of the legislation which would give them the benefits to which I think they are entitled as far as income tax is concerned. Other hon. members of this house have indicated their support for the present motion. I believe the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Watson) who seconded the motion has some observations to make on it and no doubt others will find it worthy of their support.

speakeroldname: Mr. E. J. Benson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Moose Mountain (Mr. Southam) for having brought up this interesting question, one which has of course been considered over the years by the officials who are dealing with these matters and by the government in its position of responsibility for proposing changes to the Income Tax Act.
I was very interested in the outline the hon. member gave of the important developments in Saskatchewan leading to the amalgamation of school units. As I understand it, a similar situation applies in other provinces of Canada; it certainly applies in my own province of Ontario. In his resolution the hon. member speaks of larger school units. This phrase might be difficult to define in terms of legislation and I think it might be made a little more clear later on. He also quoted in detail section 10 (3) of the Income Tax Act which is the relevant section when we are dealing with this matter. This section provides:
Where an elected officer of an incorporated municipality has been paid by the municipal corporation an amount as an allowance in a taxation year for expenses incident to the discharge of his

Mr. Speaker, I want to say at the outset that I have no hesitation or reservation at all in supporting the proposal made this afternoon by the hon. member for Moose Mountain (Mr. Southam). I want to state at the outset that in Alberta, where I think the setting up of what have been termed school units was pioneered, there does not appear to me to be any significant difference between the service provided by a school board or school unit trustees and that provided by municipal trustees. This is particularly true in the rural areas.
The parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) has just stated that he would welcome some information as to how expenses are now being paid to the elected representatives of school divisions. I would like to tell him one or two things about this matter as it applies in Alberta. I speak specifically of southern Alberta, but I think it is true for the whole province, because at this stage all the rural areas of Alberta are in what we call school divisions and I think we can put exactly the same connotation on that as you can on the words "larger school units" in the resolution. There is provision for the payment of something like $15 a day, I believe, for each one of the trustees for the days they actually spend in school board meetings, plus an allowance of something like 12 cents per mile, I believe it is at the present time, for travelling to the meetings and back to their homes. In addition to that there are special payments for occasions when a school board member is required to visit a school within his subdivision but which is many miles from his home. In these cases exactly the same allowances are paid; $15 a day for the time he must spend away from home plus 12 cents a mile travelling to and from his residence.
There is one other point I should like to bring up to show the injustice and anomaly created by section 10(3). Commencing in 1936 or 1937 Alberta set up these larger school units for the more efficient operation of schools in the rural areas. This has worked so satisfactorily that from time to time other provinces have adopted the same method.

Income Tax Act
Now we have moved to another phase and we are setting up counties. We have well over 20 counties now and these county councils administer the affairs of all the schools within their boundaries through what they call the school committee of the county council. From my interpretation of what is now provided in subsection (3) I would presume that those members who are in fact elected to the county council, even though they may be subsequently appointed by the county council to the school committee, would be able to claim under this section expenses they incur for doing exactly the same thing which the school trustees do in units which are not counties.
This is completely unfair because, as I said, they are doing exactly the same thing. I know that in some of the county councils, while the members appointed to the school committee do have a vote on the council when the council is in what might be called plenary session, they spend all or almost all of their time on school affairs. The chairmanship of the school committee is a fulltime job within that time devoted to county and school business. The chairman is completely or almost completely concerned with school affairs in the same way as the chairman of the school board. Therefore there is an injustice created here which could be corrected bv accepting the recommendation which has been made by the hon. member for Moose Mountain.
In many cases the amount of the budget and the amount of the detailed work and general responsibilities of school trustees within a given area is substantially higher than that of the municipal councillors within the same area. I think it speaks for itself that there is therefore real justification for making some changes. In fact, at the present time if we had to choose between whether the school trustee or the county councillor should receive some consideration by way of expenses incurred, there are many places where the school trustee would be given priority because of the larger amount of money which he would be handling, and the greater responsibility he has to attend to the details of school administration.
I do not wish to say more because other hon. members would like to participate in this debate, but I am pleased to hear that the parliamentary secretary is going to take this matter to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) and his officials when they are considering amendments to the Income Tax Act because, as I said, a serious injustice prevails here which could and should be corrected.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words in support of this motion moved by the hon. member for Moose Mountain (Mr. Southam). I believe this is a question of the income tax laws not keeping up with progress in some of the provinces. The hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson) illustrated this when he referred to what happened in Alberta in 1936 or 1937. The larger school unit act came into effect in Saskatchewan in 1945. I believe the motion speaks for itself when it says the government should consider-
-the advisability of amending the Income Tax Act, section (10) subsection (3) so that elected trustees of "larger school units" be entitled to the same exemptions of their regular indemnities for income tax purposes as those presently allowed to elected members of municipal corporations.
When we speak in the rural part of Saskatchewan of municipal corporations, we are naturally thinking of the rural municipalities which were set up in 1905 when the province was established. These areas are 18 miles square and have six board members and one reeve. Under the larger school unit act of Saskatchewan these boards also have a chairman elected from the six members, and these people represent an area which would be possibly six or seven times the size of a rural municipality. One way to compare this would be that an assessment in a rural municipality would be anywhere from $2 million to $4 or $5 million. An assessment in a larger school unit would run anywhere from $20 million to $25 million. These board members have to travel

and I have had the pleasure of serving on both types of board-anywhere from 30, 40 and up to 50 miles to one meeting. When I served on a local municipal council I had to travel only ten miles to qualify for expenses, yet under the larger school unit act, or under the Alberta county system, I would have to travel a great many miles but would not be entitled to this exemption. I think this is merely a matter of the government's sitting down and taking a look at section 10(3) and bringing it up to date so as to cover, as was originally intended by the act, municipal corporations.
The hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Benson) gave the house a little more information, but I can tell him that in the larger school units in Saskatchewan the members of the board receive in the neighbourhood of $300 to $400 in a year-and I have had more than $500-as their indemnity and mileage combined. This is arrived at on the basis of a per diem of $15 a day for a maximum of 15 or 16 meetings, plus the mileage expenses of the individual member concerned. Our mileage rate is 11 cents a mile, and that also can be figured out on the

same basis. As I mentioned before, this is merely a case of the government sitting down and bringing the Income Tax Act up to date so as to keep abreast of the progress which has been made, in this particular case, in Saskatchewan under their larger school unit act. However, I feel it is an injustice to the members who serve on these boards.
In the same way as the hon. member for Medicine Hat has mentioned, we in the province of Saskatchewan were in the midst of setting up counties a year or two ago, and my interpretation would be that if these counties had been set up the members of the school boards would not be entitled to an exemption because they would come under the larger school units. In closing, I would like to say I hope the government and members of the house will support this notice of motion. If it would be of any assistance to the parliamentary secretary or to the minister, I would be only too happy to sit down and talk the matter over with them. Again I urge all members to support the motion.

Mr. Speaker, I think one could almost say in one sentence all that needs to be said regarding the principle of this private member's notice of motion. We agree that there should be uniformity in the matter of exemptions to taxpayers in similar circumstances. However, when you stop to take a look at the drafting of an appropriate statute, and you take a look at the wide variety of arrangements that exist throughout Canada, you quickly see it is extremely important that some homework be done in the Department of Finance. I believe this homework will be done, as was suggested by the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance a few moments ago.
I share the gratification expressed by other members of the house that this will be done, and I shall be watching the progress made in that direction. However, it is apparent it will be necessary to have some conversations with provincial departments of education. Further, before we come to formal passage of a motion of this kind, we must inquire whether the royal commission on taxation has undertaken studies with respect to exemptions. I believe hon. members will find that the commission has been looking with some interest at all exemptions.
It finally comes back to what I said at the outset, that there is a great deal of homework to be done because of the variety of arrangements between elected boards and appointed boards. In the city of Halifax we have one school board, yet within our school system we have a tradition whereby we have
Income Tax Act
a parochial system, rather loosely put together but nevertheless very satisfactory to all concerned.
This system has been in operation for some hundred years, but there is only the one tax source. The city pays 85 per cent of the school budget and the remaining 15 per cent is paid in the form of provincial grants. Half of the members of the board are appointed by the province, and the other half by the city council of Halifax.
Those members of the school board who are elected members of the city council do not receive any remuneration from the school board, but those who are appointed by the province receive an honorarium of something like $300 per annum. Some people who are quite happy and anxious to serve on these large school units are not anxious to engage in the elective processes to either school boards, city councils, or county councils, and many of them even resent being paid for this kind of duty.
There is no doubt many of them are people in the higher income brackets, who feel they can afford to do this sort of thing, but they do not want to engage in other political activities. There is no doubt that because they are in the higher income tax brackets an exemption would be more valuable to them, but we have to take a look at the number of arrangements throughout Canada which would be involved in an extension of this particular exemption.
There are 12,000 school areas in Canada. One hon. member referred to Saskatchewan. I understand it has a more complex scheme, with large units divided into five or six subunits, and the representatives to the large units are elected by the ratepayers of the sub-units. As in Alberta, there are also separate school boards.
Manitoba has a mixed system of large and small units, and the Atlantic provinces have been moving for some years toward a system of larger units. In the western provinces election of school trustees by ratepayers is the rule, whereas in the Atlantic provinces appointment of trustees by municipal councils or the lieutenant governors is more general.
Then we come to Quebec where we find that the Roman Catholic school administration is based on the parish, except in large centres, and the Roman Catholic school boards number about 1,500. Up to the present, and I understand this is subject to change under Quebec's bill No. 60, Protestant schools have local elected representative administration in rural areas, but larger units are also being organized. Trustees are locally elected, except in Montreal and Quebec city where the school trustees are appointed, the Protestant trustees

Income Tax Act
being appointed by the lieutenant governor and the city, and the Roman Catholic trustees by the lieutenant governor and the archbishops.
Ontario has 4,200 local school boards, including 700 separate school boards and 300 secondary school boards. There are also boards of education which look after both the public and the secondary schools. Most local rural school boards are elected by ratepayers. Rural district high school area boards are appointed by councils in participating areas, and secondary school boards are appointed. Now it becomes a nice question-
Would the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.

Is there really any difference between school board trustees being elected or appointed? Whether they belong to separate school boards or public school boards they all have some expense involved in the performance of their public duties, and should there not be some provision in the Income Tax Act to take care of these expenses?

I agree generally in principle, but if you look at the notice of motion it says:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of amending the Income Tax Act, section (10) subsection (3) so that elected trustees of "larger school units" be entitled to the same exemptions of their regular indemnities for income tax purposes as those presently allowed to elected members of municipal corporations.
It specifically deals with elected members, and I was pointing out that because of the variety of methods by which trustees are elected and appointed, one should do some homework on the very point which the hon. gentleman raises. It may very well be that if you receive an honorarium from a school board, and if some portion is to be designated, the same as applies to municipal councillors, it should be generally applied regardless of whether you are elected or appointed.
Some will argue that the elected representative is under expense by virtue of the process through which he gets on the board, and because of this fact he should be granted an exemption. Some will argue this. Others will contend, as the hon. member has just done, that it really does not make much difference. But I think there is a difference between the situation confronting the person seeking election to a public office and that of one who does not have any expense by reason of being appointed by the governor in council or by some regional board, depending upon the arrangements in each province.
I can only conclude, Mr. Speaker, that there is an inconsistency in regard to the matter set out in the motion. Certainly the

matter needs attention. We should not allow the situation to continue without investigating to see whether we can arrive at a uniform policy. I am glad, as I said earlier, that the parliamentary secretary proposes to undertake the essential homework to bring about a method more appropriate and more in keeping with the views expressed by hon. members today than would be the case if we passed this motion, because if we did so the impression might be given that it was the wish of the house that any such exemptions should be restricted solely to elected trustees of larger school units.
I have mentioned that perhaps there should be some consultation with the provincial authorities. If there is any field in which there seems to be great sensitivity, and with justification, it is that which involves the provision of educational facilities within a province. Certainly anything that has to do with inducing people to undertake duties by virtue of federal income tax exemptions in the performance of such duties is a matter which should be the subject of consultation with the provinces. It should not be a difficult matter to resolve, but I should like to see that done. I share the feelings of hon. members who have so expressed themselves that it would be a good thing for the parliamentary secretary to undertake the proper homework and bring in appropriate amendments. I do not think the royal commission needs to deal with such a matter unless it has been the subject of special reference to them.

Mr. Speaker, I do not think there is any question that those of us who have served in the past on municipal councils or school boards, where most of us started our humble careers, are sympathetic with the subject matter and the understanding envisaged in the general tenor of this motion. In my view, if our free society is to work effectively, and possibly even to survive in the competitive world of today from the point of view of modes of government and modes of people determining their destinies, there is no question but that we certainly need a high level of participation by our people in our system of government, whether in the parliamentary field, local political associations or bodies such as school boards and municipal councils.
I believe the late President Kennedy put this premise better than any of us can when he said that a free society cannot survive if those who believe in that free society sit on the sidelines and merely watch the game. If there is any need today, not only in this country but throughout the free world, it is the need for participation in various aspects

of the public weal by the very best people we can possibly entice to undertake such efforts.
Far from the least of our needs is that in the realm of education. I do not know about the situation in other provinces. Our constitutional system being what it is, I am not too well versed in the manner in which education is administered in other provinces. In the province of Ontario the principle of local autonomy has been maintained to a very large degree throughout the years. However, in the province of Ontario we find that centralization is creeping into education more and more, be it for better or for worse, and that the principles of local autonomy, which have been the very basis of our education system since the days of Ryerson, are gradually being whittled away, with the result that in the not too distant future education may have a far more centralized focal point than has been the case in the past.
But so long as local autonomy is maintained to any degree in the educational system of Ontario, so long will there be a need to induce the very best and most capable people we can find to enter the field of education at the local level. This, of course, involves several spheres. Certainly from both a moral and an economic point of view we need to encourage the very best people we can to enter the teaching profession, on which rests to the largest degree the education of our young people. But at the administrative level also we need to do all we can to encourage the best people to take part as school trustees and in other fields of school administration, so that our schools will be well administered and so that the dollars and cents aspect of education will be adequately looked after.
So far as the teaching profession is concerned, which is essential to the future of education, I think there may be some troubles ahead. The teaching profession appears to be very disturbed today with regard to its future. The other day we heard the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher), who speaks so often and so loudly in the house, take umbrage over the fact that the teaching profession was disturbed at the present time because its members had been requested by the Department of Labour to fill out the cards associated with the coming pension plan. Apparently the Ontario teachers federation has taken a strong lobbyist stand in this regard. The hon. member felt that this was improper and that it was a tragic thing that the teaching profession should be taking this view.
I suggest that in taking this view the teaching profession was objecting to only one thing. As a profession I do not think its members have ever been loath to carry their weight or
Income Tax Act
to fulfil their responsibilities to society in general. However, I believe that they are objecting to being treated differently from other professions. I think they are right in this stand. I do not believe there is any more noble calling or loftier profession than that of teaching, whereby the aspirations of tomorrow will be fulfilled if they are to be fulfilled.
I certainly disagree most emphatically with the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) in this regard. There should be no distinction or no differentiation between the medical profession, the legal profession and the teaching profession in so far as the laws of this country are concerned, be they income tax, unemployment insurance or any other laws.
I think possibly the criticism of the hon. member was justified to some degree, but only in this regard-

I rise on a point of order, Mr. Speaker. I think the member has been directing his remarks during the last five or six minutes to a point which has no relevancy whatever to the notice of motion moved by the hon. member for Moose Mountain.

Speaking to the point of order, I would point out that the relevancy of my remarks is in this vein: I maintain I am attempting to establish the point that there are two facets to the question of education, the trustees on the one hand-that is the administration-and on the other hand the teaching profession. I am attempting to establish the point that on these two aspects of the problem of education, particularly teaching, rest the future effectiveness of education.
In that regard, Mr. Speaker, I am merely saying that in so far as the teaching profession is concerned, which is one aspect, I think it should be pointed out that contrary to some opinion there has been no attempt made by this house under the unemployment insurance regulations to include the teachers. There was a suggestion of this type made in the Gill report, but any qualms the teaching profession may have in this regard are unfounded. In so far as this government or this house is concerned, we have not treated them in any way differently from any other profession. I do not believe the day will come when this government or this house will see fit to do so, even though the Gill report may have suggested it. I do suggest that in so far as the teaching profession is concerned, this house has maintained its respect for the profession and has legislated in no way that would diminish the honour of that profession.
Now, in so far as the trustees are concerned, if I may be permitted to turn to that specific aspect of my hon. friend's motion,

Business of the House
I	would say that apparently he is concerned about the trustees of the larger school units.
I look somewhat askance at my hon. friend because normally I would have thought he would have been somewhat concerned with the larger and bigger, but also with the smaller and humble. I do believe this party professes to speak not so much for Bay street as for the little man. I am somewhat surprised to see that his motion refers only to the larger school units and, in particular, to those trustees who are apparently elected to school units rather than appointed, as is the case in the smaller areas.
In the part of the country from which I come, school boards are of two types. Some boards are elected and some of them are appointed. District schools, which today I think are generally accepted as important throughout Ontario, are the trend today. I have recently had occasion to see something of the school question in Manitoba. In that province I think the trend is to centralize the district schools and bring the boy or girl from the country into the larger school units in those areas. In Ontario, certainly in eastern Ontario, the area school trustees are appointed by the local council and by the local school boards, separate and public, to serve on this area school board.
The problems of these area school boards I assure you, Mr. Speaker, are certainly not less, and in fact in a very large measure are far greater than those of the elected school boards. Where urban and rural areas are concerned, the problems are different. Frequently there is difficulty with the problem of equalization of assessment in these areas. I know of no more difficult area of public service than service on one of these area school boards. I know these men sit many nights during the month into the small hours, and they have all the problems connected with running very large business entities, because these school boards are big business.
In my own town of Arnprior, which is a town of some 5,500 people, the high school has an enrolment of nearly 1,000 boys and
girls. I think this points up the fact that those who serve on these school boards, and who serve as teachers, have very important work, and that those who serve on these appointed school boards have work that is just as important as those who are elected representatives. While I agree most wholeheartedly with the general principle of this resolution, I should be most remiss in my duty to those people who serve on the school boards in my area if I did not insist that if any consideration is to be given in respect of income tax deductions, as suggested by the resolution, it should be given not only to those who are elected but also to those who are appointed to serve on school boards. It may be that if our energies are directed toward this problem, we should see that all school boards will be treated equally.
